n: Zophar, the third and bluntest friend, gives his second (and last) speech. He seems to ignore Job’s great statement of faith in chapter 19.

f.g: From Naamah, a place of uncertain location, perhaps in Arabia.

n: Zophar says his troubled thoughts push him to answer quickly.

f.g: Literally “because of my inner agitation” — he is upset and eager to reply.

n: He feels insulted by Job’s rebuke, and his understanding compels him to respond.

f.g: A rebuke that insults me — perhaps Job’s warning in 19:28-29.

n: Zophar appeals to what everyone has known since humans first lived on earth.

f.w: since man was placed upon earth
f.g: Literally “since Adam was placed on earth.”

n: His thesis: the triumph of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment. There is truth here — Job’s mistake is in being labeled wicked.

f.w: the triumphing of the wicked is short

n: Even if the wicked man’s pride rises to the sky and his head touches the clouds…

f.w: his head reach unto the clouds

n: …he will perish like his own dung, and those who knew him will ask, “Where did he go?” Zophar’s language is deliberately crude.
He will vanish like a dream when you wake up, chased away like a vision of the night.
No eye that saw him will see him again; his home will know him no more.

f.w: neither shall his place any more behold him

n: His children will have to beg favor from the poor, and he will have to give back what he took by force.
His body may be full of youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.

f.g: Better “his youthful vigor” — the Hebrew word means youthfulness.

n: Zophar compares wickedness to a sweet treat that someone savors, rolling it under the tongue.
The wicked person loves sin so much he holds it in his mouth and won’t let it go.

f.g: Hold on to it, be reluctant to give it up.

n: But in his stomach the sweet food turns sour, becoming poison like snake venom.
He gulps down riches but will vomit them up — God makes him disgorge them.
What he swallowed becomes snake poison that kills him. Sin carries its own deadly consequences.

f.g: Ancient people thought snakes struck with their tongues.

n: He will never enjoy the streams of honey and butter — images of plenty in a blessed land.

f.g: Butter = curds or cream; images of abundance.

n: He must give back what he gained and cannot enjoy the profits of his trading.
Zophar names the crime: crushing and abandoning the poor and seizing houses he did not build.

f.w: oppressed and hath forsaken the poor

n: Because his greed is never satisfied, he will never know inner peace, and nothing he craves will be saved.

f.g: Contentment; his appetite is never satisfied.

n: Nothing escapes his appetite, so his prosperity will not last.

f.w: There shall none of his meat be left
f.g: He devours everything, leaving nothing behind.

n: At the height of his plenty, distress overtakes him, and every hand of misery strikes him.

f.g: In distress, in a tight place.

n: While he is filling his belly, God rains down his fury like a storm — an ironic “meal” of judgment.
He may run from an iron weapon, but a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him.
The arrow is pulled out through his body, gleaming, and terrors come over him.

f.g: Liver or gallbladder — the arrow has pierced him through.

n: Total darkness waits for his treasures; a fire no human lit consumes him and whatever remains in his tent.

f.g: A fire not fanned by human breath — fire from God.

n: Heaven exposes his guilt and the earth rises as a witness against him. This seems to reply to Job’s hope for a heavenly witness (16:19).

f.w: The heaven shall reveal his iniquity

n: His household’s wealth will be carried off like a flood on the day of God’s anger.

f.g: Be swept away like rushing water.

n: Zophar sums up: this is God’s assigned portion for the wicked. His words are true of evil in general but cruelly misapplied to Job.

f.w: the heritage appointed unto him by God
